title: The Koh-i-Noor
hook: the great diamond comes to Lahore in 1813 from an exiled Afghan king

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peshawar, the city at the mouth of the pass, and your line, the edge. Today, something small enough to hold in one hand.

A king without a kingdom arrives in Lahore. He's Shah Shuja, once ruler in Kabul, now driven out, with his family and what's left of his treasure. He needs shelter and help. And he carries one stone that had passed from ruler to ruler, a diamond so large it had its own name. The Maharaja wants it. The exile doesn't want to let it go, and he has nowhere else to turn.
screen: `AN EXILED KING IN LAHORE.` → `ONE STONE WITH ITS OWN NAME.` → `WHO WILL HOLD IT?`

segments.voice: Koh-i-Noor is Persian, usually given as the mountain of light: a stone named like a mountain. How it changed hands, the histories don't agree on every detail, and Afghan and Sikh accounts tell it differently. As it's usually told, Shah Shuja and his wife had come to the Maharaja for help, and the diamond became the price of that help. Some accounts say it was handed over under pressure, after delay and hard bargaining. So the stone came to Lahore not in a battle but in a bargain with a man who had little left to bargain with. That's worth sitting with. Tradition says the Maharaja wore it on his arm in an armband and showed it at court on great days. It became part of how Lahore looked to visitors: a kingdom that could hold what Kabul and Delhi had held before. Underneath sits a question: what counts as a jewel? In Guru Nanak's hymns, jewels can stand for something inside. In the Japji, he says the mind holds jewels, gems and rubies, if you listen to even one teaching of the Guru. A king's diamond is real, beautiful, and worth a fortune. The Gurus point at a different kind of worth. Both stand in today's story, side by side.
screen: `THE MOUNTAIN OF LIGHT.` · `A BARGAIN WITH AN EXILE.` · `WORN ON THE MAHARAJA'S ARM.` · `THE JEWEL THE GURUS POINT TO.` · then, large: `WHAT IS PRECIOUS.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself, without rushing, what you'd call precious; let the first answers come and go, and wait for the quieter ones underneath: a person, a memory, a kind of peace no one could buy from you. Choose one and hold it in your mind the way you'd hold a stone in your palm, turning it to the light. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
The Koh-i-Noor. The mountain of light, the great diamond that came to Lahore from an exiled king, and that the Maharaja wore on his arm.
Your line: what is precious. Some jewels never fit in an armband. Day nine hundred nineteen, done.

screen: `DAY 919 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A COURT OF MANY FAITHS.`
